A chocolate company's promotional egg just set an auction record most jewellery houses would take.

The 22-carat gold 'Conundrum' egg, made by Garrard & Co. in 1983 for a Cadbury's treasure hunt, sold for £123,500 (about $166,600) at Batemans Auctioneers on 1 August — close to six times its pre-sale estimate and a world auction record for a bejewelled egg of its type, per Forbes.

The number worth holding against it is the metal. The catalogue puts the egg at 323.6 grams of 22-carat gold — roughly 9.54 troy ounces of pure gold. At $4,341.30 an ounce, this desk's tape close on the day, that is about $41,400 of bullion, derived from the stated weight and fineness.

The record is four times the metal. The rest — more than $125,000 of it — is signature, provenance and a hallmark. Gold at record levels has quietly changed what an auction result means: the metal is now the smaller part of the record, and for anyone consigning this autumn, the paperwork is worth assembling before the estimate is agreed.

The gap between what gold costs in China and what a jewellery counter charges for it is 348 yuan a gram.

The Shanghai Gold Exchange's Au99.99 contract traded at 938 yuan a gram on the morning of 8 August. The same day, Chow Tai Fook listed 24-carat jewellery at 1,286 yuan a gram, Chow Sang Sang at 1,285, Lukfook at 1,284, Lao Feng Xiang and Lao Miao at 1,283, Zhou Liu Fu at 1,281 — every major brand within five yuan of every other, roughly 37% above the exchange benchmark.

What changed this week is the direction of travel. On 6 August the major brands raised counter prices by close to 60 yuan a gram in a single session, against a benchmark that moved a fraction of that. The counter is no longer following the benchmark. It is running ahead of it.

The backdrop: China's first-half gold jewellery consumption fell almost 34% by weight this year, while bar and coin demand rose over 28%. A counter charging 37% over spot into a shrinking jewellery market isn't holding that margin out of confidence — it's holding it because the fixed cost of a branded retail network doesn't fall when tonnage does.

Kalyan Jewellers reported consolidated revenue of ₹10,589 crore for the quarter to 30 June, up 46% year on year, and net profit up 32% to ₹349 crore.

The line that should interest the rest of the trade isn't on the profit statement. Kalyan's gold-recirculation campaign, run as 'Shine with India', contributed more than 46% of revenue across the quarter — and more than 55% in the month of June alone. That is not a promotion. It is a sourcing strategy, and on the June figure it is the larger half of the business.

The volume backdrop explains why. Indian gold jewellery demand fell 15% by weight this quarter, its lowest second quarter since the pandemic, even as the value of that demand rose about 50%. Kalyan's own same-store sales grew about 28% — the honest comparison, and still comfortably ahead of the market.

With gold above $4,300 an ounce, the binding constraint on an Indian jeweller isn't demand for finished pieces — it's access to metal that doesn't have to be imported at duty and financed at working-capital rates. The household is the cheapest supplier in the country, and Kalyan is now running that supply chain on purpose.
